title: A stage-by-stage fit comparison asks: which stage or solver actually moved the model toward the data?
summary: Several ignition-delay curves are overlaid: the nominal mechanism, the result after each optimization stage, and sometimes the result from different solvers. The legends carry an error number for each curve. The figure is read by checking, condition by condition, whether the printed number and the visible distance to the data agree and whether each stage helped.

media.alt: Ignition delay in milliseconds on a log axis against 1000/T for n-heptane at phi 1, with experiments at 13.5 and 42 atm as markers with error bars. For each pressure a dash-dot nominal line, a solid GA line and a dotted SLSQP line are drawn, with a legend printing a chi-square number beside each. The curves bend and flatten in the middle of the temperature range.

source.caption: GA vs SLSQP solver comparison — n-heptane
source.note: n-heptane optimization at phi=1, comparing a genetic-algorithm (global, derivative-free) solver against gradient-based SLSQP — checking that both solvers converge to the same physically consistent answer rather than one finding an artifact of its own search method.
group: 08_nheptane_phi1_GAvsSLSQP: GA vs SLSQP solver comparison — n-heptane

read_the_figure.question: How does the agreement with ignition-delay data change from the nominal mechanism to each optimization stage, and does it change with the solver?
read_the_figure.axes: x: 1000/T in 1/K (temperature falls to the right). y: ignition delay in milliseconds on a log axis. Markers with vertical bars: experiments with their error bars, one marker style and colour per pressure (and per equivalence ratio where several are shown). Lines: dash-dot is the nominal mechanism, dotted the first stage, solid the second stage (in the five-panel figure), or solid for the genetic algorithm and dotted for SLSQP (in the solver figure). The legend prints an error number beside each curve.
look_at: Group the curves by colour (one colour is one pressure). Within one colour compare the line styles: this is the effect of the stage or solver for that single condition.

Check each printed number against the picture. A curve closer to the markers should carry a smaller number. If it does not, the number is measuring something different from what the eye sees (for example it weights points differently).
Look for conditions where a later stage is worse than the nominal one: a larger printed number or a visibly larger gap. These are the conditions the optimization traded away.
In the solver figure, compare solid and dotted lines of the same colour with the markers. The figure shows whether the two solvers agree on a result, which the printed numbers also report.
Look at the shape of the data against the shape of the curves: a flat or bent stretch in the data (a change of chemistry with temperature) that a curve does not follow.
read_the_figure.proves: How each stage or solver changed the fit to the data that were in the objective, condition by condition, as the printed numbers state. It shows no more than that: it does not show that a stage is generally better, and the printed numbers are the figure's own measure of fit.
if_wrong: A later-stage number larger than the nominal one for a condition: the optimization worsened that condition. The aggregate objective can still improve.
Two solvers giving clearly different numbers: they have found different parameter sets, or one is stuck in a local minimum. A statement that they 'agree' needs the numbers to agree.
Stage-1 and stage-2 lines on top of each other: the second stage changed nothing visible for that condition.
Different error measures in different figures (here a chi-square-like number in one and an epsilon in others): the numbers cannot be compared across figures unless the definition is the same.
must_check: The definition of each printed error number (the solver figure gives a formula; the other figures do not define epsilon on the figure itself).
A legend whose entries are grouped by condition and in the same order for every condition.
Log y axis and units on both axes.
The same experimental points under all curves.
Whether the conditions shown are the ones used in the objective or held out.

terms.meaning: One run of the tuning procedure. Later stages start from the result of earlier ones and usually use more or different targets.

A genetic algorithm is a stochastic, gradient-free population method that searches globally. SLSQP, sequential least-squares programming, is a gradient-based local method that follows the slope from its starting point.
The mean of squared residuals divided by the measurement uncertainty. A value near one means the model misses by about one uncertainty on average.
The mechanism with its original rate parameters, before tuning.
Time from the start until ignition is detected, in milliseconds.
A local method ends in the valley it starts in; a global one tries to compare valleys. Different methods can end at different parameter sets from the same start.

remember: Compare curves of the same colour: that holds the condition fixed.
A printed number is only comparable to another that uses the same definition.
Chi-square near one means a miss of about one uncertainty per point.
A stage can improve the aggregate and worsen some conditions.
A local solver and a global solver can disagree on the same problem.

understand.title: Why overlay the stages
understand.text: The final fit alone hides how it was reached. Overlaying the nominal, first and second stage shows which conditions the first stage fixed, which only the second changed, and which were never improved.

understand.title: Why two solvers
understand.text: A global solver and a gradient-based one can reach different parameters. Plotting both on the same data is a sanity check: if they agree, the answer is robust to the search method; if not, the printed numbers say by how much they disagree, and the better one is the one with the lower error.

understand.title: The three figures of this group
understand.text: The first figure has five panels, one per equivalence ratio, for n-heptane, with the nominal, stage-1 and stage-2 curves and an epsilon beside each. The second shows n-heptane at one equivalence ratio and two pressures with the two solvers. The third shows 1,3-butadiene at one equivalence ratio and three pressures across the stages. Read them as three views of the same question, with the printed numbers as the figure's own scores.

steps.title: Chi-square per point
steps.note: This is the formula printed in the solver figure's legend. Each residual is measured in units of its measurement uncertainty and squared, so large misses count much more than small ones.

steps.title: Relation to a 10 percent uncertainty
steps.note: If the uncertainty is 10 percent of the delay, the chi-square per point is 100 times the mean squared relative error. A relative error of 15 percent on every point would give 2.25. Whether that uncertainty is the one used in the figure is not stated; it is shown here as an illustration.

steps.title: Improvement ratio between two curves
steps.note: Below 1 the tuned curve fits better, above 1 worse. It is the right quantity to compare conditions with different nominal errors.

steps.title: A local descent ends in its own basin
steps.note: A gradient-based method finishes in the valley where it started. A population-based global method can end in a different, lower one, which is why the two can differ on the same problem.

steps.title: Why straight lines cannot follow a bend
steps.note: A single activation energy gives a straight line. The curved or flat stretches in the data have a changing apparent activation energy, which a mechanism with the wrong balance of chemistry cannot reproduce by retuning one set of rates.

worked.title: Which solver did better, as a ratio
worked.problem: At phi = 1, 13.5 atm the legend prints nominal 17.047, GA 5.309 and SLSQP 19.822. At 42 atm it prints 34.452, 15.498 and 23.874. Compute each solver's ratio to nominal.
worked.answer: By the printed numbers GA cuts the error to 31 and 45 percent of nominal, SLSQP reaches 69 percent at 42 atm but is 16 percent worse than nominal at 13.5 atm. The two solvers do not give the same answer in the printed numbers; the project page's caption says they are compared to check agreement, and the owner should confirm what is meant.

analyze.q: A later stage has a larger printed number than the nominal for one pressure but a smaller number for another. What does that say about the objective?
analyze.hint: It sums over conditions; a trade-off is allowed.

analyze.q: Stage-1 and stage-2 curves lie on top of each other in most panels. What does this say about the second stage?
analyze.hint: What it changed, and which conditions it could not touch.

analyze.q: The solver figure shows both solvers following the data's flat stretch only partly. What could be missing from the model rather than from the optimization?
analyze.hint: A regime of chemistry that no retuning of the included parameters can create.

evaluate.q: Is it legitimate to say 'both solvers converge to the same answer' on this evidence?
evaluate.hint: Compare the printed numbers of the two solvers.

evaluate.q: The error numbers use different definitions in different figures. How would you make the figures comparable?
evaluate.hint: Use one definition, print its formula, and quote the same measure in every legend.

create: Redraw the stage figure as small multiples with one panel per pressure and a bar of the printed number for each stage underneath.
Design a test that shows whether the two solvers find the same parameter set: what would you compare, besides the curves?

checks.q: Why compare lines of the same colour?
checks.answer: One colour is one pressure (one condition). Comparing line styles within a colour holds the condition fixed so only the stage or solver changes.

checks.q: Nominal 20.0 and tuned 5.0. What is the ratio?
checks.answer: 5.0 / 20.0 = 0.25: the tuned error is a quarter of nominal.

checks.q: A tuned curve is farther from the data than nominal. Is the optimization wrong?
checks.answer: Not necessarily. The aggregate objective can improve while some conditions get worse; but those conditions should be listed and explained.

checks.q: Two solvers give 5.3 and 19.8 on the same data. Which would you use?
checks.hint: Lower is better, but check the definition.
checks.answer: The one with the lower error, provided both use the same definition and the same data. A large gap also says that at least one solver is not at the optimum and that the search is sensitive to the method.

checks.q: What would show that the second stage improves prediction, not only fit?
checks.answer: Plot the nominal, first-stage and second-stage curves on conditions not used in any stage and report the same error measure there.
